paragraphs: “Now I understand the first half,” said Alyosha.
“You understand the first half. That half was a drama, and it was played out there. The second half is a tragedy, and it’s being acted out here.”
“And so far I don’t understand anything of that second half,” said Alyosha.
“And me? Do you think I understand it?”
“Wait, Dmitri. There’s one important question. Tell me, you were engaged, and you’re still engaged?”

“We weren’t engaged right away, not until three months after that adventure. The next day I told myself the whole business was over and done with, and there would be no sequel. It seemed caddish to make her an offer. For her part, she gave no sign of life during the six weeks she stayed in town, except for one thing. The day after her visit, the maid slipped round with an envelope addressed to me. I tore it open. It held the change from the banknote. Only four thousand five hundred roubles had been needed, but changing it had cost a discount of about two hundred. So she sent me only about two hundred and sixty. I don’t remember exactly. But not a note, not a word of explanation. I searched the packet for a pencil mark—n-nothing! Well, I spent the rest of the money on such an orgy that the new major had to reprimand me.

“Well, then the lieutenant-colonel produced the battalion money, to everyone’s astonishment, because nobody believed he still had it untouched. No sooner had he paid it than he fell ill and took to his bed. Three weeks later softening of the brain set in, and five days after that he died. He was buried with military honors, since he hadn’t had time to get his discharge. Ten days after the funeral, Katerina Ivanovna went off to Moscow with her aunt and her sister. And look what happened: on the very day they left (I hadn’t seen them, didn’t see them off or say goodbye) I received a tiny note, a sheet of thin blue paper, with just one line in pencil: ‘I will write to you. Wait. K.’ And that was all.

“I’ll explain the rest now in two words. In Moscow their fortunes changed with lightning speed, as unexpectedly as in an Arabian fairy tale. That general’s widow, their nearest relation, suddenly lost the two nieces who were her heiresses and next of kin—both died in the same week of smallpox. The old lady was prostrated with grief. She welcomed Katya as a daughter, as her one hope, clung to her, and changed her will in Katya’s favor. But that concerned the future. Meanwhile she gave her eighty thousand roubles for present use, as a marriage portion, to do with as she liked. She was a hysterical woman. I saw something of her in Moscow, later.

“Well, and then suddenly I received four thousand five hundred roubles by post. I was speechless with surprise, as you can imagine. Three days later the promised letter came. I have it on me right now. You have to read it. She offers to be my wife, offers herself to me. ‘I love you madly,’ she says, ‘even if you don’t love me, never mind. Be my husband. Don’t be afraid. I won’t hamper you in any way. I will be your chattel. I will be the carpet under your feet. I want to love you forever. I want to save you from yourself.’ Alyosha, I’m not worthy to repeat those lines in my vulgar words and my vulgar tone, my everlastingly vulgar tone that I can never cure myself of. That letter stabs me even now. Do you think I don’t mind—that I don’t mind still? I wrote her an answer at once, since I couldn’t possibly go to Moscow. I wrote to her in tears. There’s one thing I’ll be ashamed of forever: I referred to her being rich and having a dowry, while I was only a stuck-up beggar! I mentioned money! I should have borne it in silence, but it slipped from my pen. Then I wrote straight away to Ivan and told him all I could about it in a letter of six pages, and sent him to her. Why do you look like that? Why are you staring at me? Yes, Ivan fell in love with her; he’s in love with her still. I know that. By the world’s judgment I did a stupid thing; but perhaps that one stupid thing may be the saving of us all now. Oo! Don’t you see how highly she thinks of Ivan, how she respects him? When she compares us, do you suppose she can love a man like me, especially after all that’s happened here?”
“But I’m convinced she does love a man like you, and not a man like him.”

“She loves her own _virtue_, not me.” The words burst out of Dmitri involuntarily, almost spitefully. He laughed, but a minute later his eyes blazed, he turned crimson and struck the table hard with his fist.

“I swear, Alyosha,” he cried, with intense and genuine anger at himself, “you may not believe me, but as God is holy and Christ is God, I swear that although I smiled at her lofty sentiments just now, I know I’m a million times baser in soul than she is, and that those lofty sentiments of hers are as sincere as a heavenly angel’s. That’s the tragedy of it—that I know that for certain. So what if someone shows off a bit? Don’t I do it myself? And yet I’m sincere, I’m sincere. As for Ivan, I can understand how he must be cursing nature now—a man with his intellect, too! To see the preference given—to whom, to what? To a monster who, though he’s engaged and all eyes are fixed on him, can’t restrain his debaucheries—and right before his fiancée’s eyes! A man like me is preferred, and he is rejected. And why? Because a girl wants to sacrifice her life and destiny out of gratitude. It’s ridiculous! I’ve never said a word of this to Ivan, and Ivan of course has never dropped a hint of it to me. But destiny will be fulfilled. The best man will hold his ground, and the undeserving one will vanish for ever into his back-alley—his filthy back-alley, his beloved back-alley, where he’s at home and where he’ll sink in filth and stench of his own free will and with enjoyment. I’ve been talking foolishly. I’ve no words left. I use them at random, but it will be as I’ve said. I’ll drown in the back-alley, and she’ll marry Ivan.”

“Wait, Dmitri,” Alyosha interrupted again, very anxious. “There’s one thing you haven’t made clear yet: you’re still engaged all the same, aren’t you? How can you break off the engagement if she, your fiancée, doesn’t want to?”

“Yes, formally and solemnly engaged. It was all done when I arrived in Moscow, with great ceremony, with ikons, all in fine style. The general’s widow blessed us and—would you believe it?—congratulated Katya. ‘You’ve made a good choice,’ she said. ‘I see right through him.’ And—would you believe it?—she didn’t like Ivan and hardly greeted him. I had long talks with Katya in Moscow. I told her about myself—sincerely, honorably. She listened to everything.
There was sweet confusion, there were tender words.
Though there were proud words as well. She wrung a mighty promise out of me to reform. I gave my promise, and here—”
“What?”
“Why, I called you and brought you out here today, this very day—remember it—to send you again, this very day, to Katerina Ivanovna, and—”
“What?”
“To tell her I’ll never come to see her again. Say, ‘He sends you his compliments.’”
“But is that possible?”
“That’s exactly why I’m sending you instead of going myself: because it’s impossible. How could I tell her myself?”
“And where are you going?”
“To the back-alley.”
“To Grushenka, then!” Alyosha exclaimed mournfully, clasping his hands. “Can Rakitin really have told the truth? I thought you had only been to see her, and that was all.”

“Can an engaged man pay such visits? Is it possible, with such a fiancée, and before the eyes of all the world? Confound it, I have some honor! The moment I began visiting Grushenka, I stopped being engaged, and stopped being an honest man. I understand that. Why are you looking at me? You see, I went there in the first place to beat her. I’d heard, and now I know for a fact, that that captain, father’s agent, had given Grushenka an I.O.U. of mine so that she could sue me for payment and put an end to me. They wanted to scare me. So I went to beat her. I’d had a glimpse of her before. She doesn’t strike you at first sight. I knew about her old merchant, who’s lying ill now, paralyzed, though he’s leaving her a decent little sum. I knew, too, that she loved money, that she hoarded it and lent it out at a wicked rate of interest, that she’s a merciless cheat and swindler. I went to beat her, and I stayed. The storm broke—it struck me down like the plague. I’m plague-stricken still, and I know that everything is over, that there will never be anything more for me. The cycle of the ages is accomplished. That’s my position. And though I’m a beggar, as fate would have it, I had three thousand in my pocket just then. I drove with Grushenka to Mokroe, a place twenty-five versts from here. I got gypsies there, and champagne, and made all the peasants drunk on it, and all the women and girls. I sent the thousands flying. In three days I was stripped bare, but a hero. Do you suppose the hero had gained his end? Not a sign of it from her. I tell you, that rogue Grushenka has a supple curve all over her body. You can see it in her little foot, even in her little toe. I saw it, and kissed it, but that was all, I swear! ‘I’ll marry you if you like,’ she said, ‘you’re a beggar, you know. Say you won’t beat me and will let me do whatever I choose, and perhaps I’ll marry you.’ She laughed, and she’s laughing still!”
